name: Nishimura-Cole Indigo Selvedge Denim Jacket
description:
A classic Type III-silhouette denim jacket cut from 14.5oz selvedge indigo denim, produced by Nishimura-Cole — a small-batch label founded by two textile engineers who left a major corponation fabric division to make things slowly and correctly. The construction is traditional: single-piece back, two chest pockets with button flaps, side cinch tabs, copper rivets at stress points. The denim is sourced from a selvedge loom operation in what used to be Osaka — one of the few remaining traditional shuttle-loom facilities — and every jacket comes with a small card describing the fabric's origin run.

This jacket fades beautifully with wear. The creases and fade lines are unique to each wearer's movement patterns — the 'whiskers' at the lap, the honeycombs at the elbow, the chest fade where your bag strap rests. Nishimura-Cole produces 150 jackets per season. They sell out. The secondhand market is active and prices hold. Tier 3 buyers who care about craft own one. Tier 4 buyers who want to signal that they care about craft own one too.
what_it_says: You understand that some things improve with time and use. You're not interested in fast fashion or fast anything. The fade on your jacket is a record of where you've been.
worn_by: anyone who found one secondhand and understood what they had
story_hooks: The Osaka loom facility that produces Nishimura-Cole's denim is under acquisition pressure from a corponation textile division. If the sale goes through, the fabric changes. The label's founders are quietly trying to buy the facility themselves and need capital they don't have.

A specific jacket from Nishimura-Cole's 2194 run — identifiable by a slight warp irregularity in the right shoulder — belonged to a journalist who disappeared while investigating Spire financial flows. The jacket was found in a Tier 2 secondhand shop. Someone wants to know how it got there.

The fade pattern on a heavily worn Nishimura-Cole jacket, photographed under specific lighting, was used as an identifier in a coded message between two people who had agreed on no other contact method. The jacket's current owner has no idea.
